concept.name: Hedger
concept.definition: A hedger is a market participant who enters into positions in a futures or other derivatives market opposite to positions held in the cash market to minimize the risk of financial loss from an adverse price change, or who buys or sells futures as a temporary substitute for a cash transaction that will occur later. One can hedge either a long cash position (e.g., owning the commodity) or a short cash position (e.g., planning to buy it later).
concept.intuition: A hedger uses the futures market like insurance: they already have real-world price exposure from their business, and they take an offsetting market position so that a bad price move hurts less.
concept.mechanics: The hedger identifies an underlying commercial exposure (inventory, future purchases or sales, borrowing costs) and takes a derivatives position whose value moves oppositely, e.g., a farmer sells grain futures against the coming harvest. The residual risk is basis risk — the risk that the cash-futures price relationship changes unexpectedly between establishing and lifting the hedge.
concept.formula: Basis = cash price - futures price; hedge effectiveness depends on the stability of the basis over the hedge horizon.
concept.failure_modes: Hedges fail through basis risk, contract mismatch (grade, location, timing), and margin-call liquidity strain when the futures leg loses cash before the offsetting physical gain is realized. Over-hedging or hedging a wrongly estimated exposure can convert a hedge into de facto speculation.
concept.misconceptions: Hedging is not about making money on the futures position — a perfect hedge transfers price risk, it does not create profit. It is also not true that hedging eliminates all risk; it exchanges outright price risk for (smaller) basis risk.
concept.example: An airline expects to buy 1 million gallons of jet fuel in three months and buys heating-oil futures as a cross-hedge; if fuel prices rise, the futures gain offsets the higher purchase cost.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
